newsitem.title: SOUTH AFRICA: Hopes rise for easing of S.Africa forex controls.
newsitem.headline: Hopes rise for easing of S.Africa forex controls.

text.p: Hopes are rising that South Africa will accelerate its plans to ease foreign exchange controls, possibly announcing moves by mid-March, analysts said on Friday.

Markets are looking for a clear statement of intent on the issue from President Nelson Mandela when he opens parliament on February 7 with more details following in Finance Minister Trevor Manuel's March 12 budget, they said.

James Cross, deputy governor of the Reserve Bank in charge of exchange control, said renewed foreign inflows and a stronger rand were encouraging signs. But he cautioned the authorities wanted to be sure that inflows were sustainable.
"If the rand stabilises at what are deemed to be fair levels, it is going to make life much easier on many fronts -- and one of them will be exchange controls," Cross told Reuters.
"But we want to be sure that the inflows are reasonably sustainable."

South Africa has removed foreign exchange controls on non-residents, but residents are still prevented from taking anything but very small amounts of currency out the country. Lifting controls too fast could trigger a flight of capital. But economists argue the move is essential to reintegrate South Africa into the world economy.
The government failed to act in late-1995, when confidence and inflows were riding high. Analysts say the government will not want to miss the boat again.
"Now would be a wonderful time to start implementing measures to relax exchange controls," said Anastasia Gekis, economist at ABN AMRO bank in Johannesburg.
"The market seems poised for it and the budget would be the ideal opportunity to do it, underlining the implementation of the government's macro-economic strategy."
Cross declined to speculate on the timing of any move but reiterated that the Reserve Bank -- which advises the finance ministry on controls -- favoured a gradualist approach.
"You need time to swap willing for unwilling investors. Therefore I feel a 'big bang' would not be advisable. It would cause major disruptions."

Government sources said Mandela's keynote February 7 address would be based on decisions taken at a four-day meeting of the African National Congress leadership earlier this month, where the leadership agreed to accelerate economic reform.
That would involve a renewed commitment to last June's economic plan, which included a pledge to gradually scrap remaining foreign exchange controls and to partially or fully privatise state assets.
Officials said the Finance Ministry was still finalising its section of the speech for the opening of parliament, but a first draft of the address would be ready by the end of the weekend.
Money market traders said current conditions were favourable for further steps to allow South African institutions and individuals to move some cash offshore.
While interest rates remained attractively high, the country should be cushioned from any excess outflows by foreign demand for South African assets, they said.
Inflows are expected to have lifted foreign exchange reserves by around one billion rand ($220 million) in January to over 11 billion rand.
"They obviously want to use any significant strength to ease up on exchange controls," said Sandra Gordon, economist at Syfrets Managed Assets in Cape Town.
"But it's not only a matter of the quantity of the capital that's coming in but also the quality of the capital. It can't be based simply on volatile portfolio flows."
So far, exchange control relaxation has focused on institutional investors who are allowed to swap up to 10 percent of their assets for foreign investments.
Concessions for funds could be increased further, but there may also be moves to help individuals -- perhaps by allowing onshore dollar bank accounts.
"That would do a lot for confidence but would maintain reserves in South Africa," said Gordon.
